mcqs.question: A backend API works correctly in isolation, and the frontend passes all its own unit tests, but users can't complete checkout because the frontend calls the API with the wrong parameter name. What kind of test is most likely to catch this?
options: A unit test on the backend, since the bug involves an API
A unit test on the frontend, since the bug involves frontend code
An e2e test, since the bug only manifests in how the real frontend and real backend are wired together
A code coverage report, since it would show which lines are untested
mcqs.explanation: Neither component is individually broken — the bug exists only in how they're wired together, which is exactly the class of bug only a test exercising the real, connected system can surface. Backend or frontend unit tests each stay within one component's boundary, and a coverage report only shows which lines executed, not whether the wiring between components is correct.

mcqs.question: Why does selecting elements by accessible role and label (`getByRole`, `getByLabel`) tend to survive UI changes better than selecting by CSS class name?
options: Role and label selectors are always faster to execute than CSS selectors
CSS class names are more likely to change during a visual redesign, while a button's accessible role and label are tied to its actual function and change less often
CSS selectors are deprecated and no longer supported by modern browsers
Role and label selectors don't require the page to have loaded first
mcqs.explanation: A visual restyle routinely renames CSS classes but rarely changes what a button is named or what role it plays for a user, so selecting by role/label is more resilient to exactly the kind of change a redesign makes. It isn't about execution speed, CSS selectors remain fully supported, and both selector types still require the element to exist on the page.

mcqs.question: A login form's HTML structure changes, and forty e2e tests across the suite call into that form directly with raw selectors. What does the Page Object pattern prevent in this situation?
options: It prevents the HTML structure from ever needing to change
It eliminates the need to update any test when the form changes, permanently
It confines the needed update to one Page Object class instead of forty scattered test files
It automatically detects and fixes broken selectors at runtime
mcqs.explanation: Wrapping the page's structure behind one class means a structural change requires updating exactly that one file, and every test using the Page Object is fixed simultaneously — it doesn't prevent change or eliminate updates entirely, and there's no runtime auto-repair involved.

mcqs.question: An e2e test intermittently fails to click a button that's clearly present when a human looks at the screenshot. What's the most likely cause?
options: The button element was deleted from the page's HTML entirely
A timing issue — the button existed in the DOM but hadn't finished rendering, animating, or becoming interactive when the test tried to click it
The test framework has a permanent bug in its click implementation
The button's accessible role was defined incorrectly in the HTML
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic e2e timing flake — the element is technically present but not yet visually stable or interactive, which is exactly why a human looking at the final rendered screenshot sees it fine. A deleted element wouldn't be visible at all, this isn't a framework-wide bug, and the role isn't inherently at fault just because a click intermittently misses.

mcqs.question: Why is a hardcoded `sleep(2000)` generally worse than an explicit wait for a specific condition in an e2e test?
options: Sleep statements are not supported in most test frameworks
A fixed sleep either wastes time when the app is ready sooner, or still fails if the app happens to be slower than the hardcoded duration on that run
Explicit waits never time out, so they are always slower
Sleep statements cause tests to pass even when the application has crashed
mcqs.explanation: A fixed sleep is a guess at duration — too short and it fails on a slow run, too long and it wastes real time on every fast run, while an explicit wait proceeds the moment its condition is actually met, up to a timeout. Sleep is fully supported by frameworks, explicit waits do have timeouts and aren't inherently slower, and neither approach masks an actual application crash.

mcqs.question: A team has been re-running failed e2e tests until they pass for months, without investigating why they fail. What's the real risk of this pattern?
options: It has no real risk as long as the suite eventually shows green
It only wastes CI compute time, with no other consequence
A genuine regression can get lost among the routine noise and be dismissed and merged the same way a flaky failure is
It will eventually cause the test framework itself to stop working
mcqs.explanation: Once ignoring red e2e results becomes normal, a real bug's failure looks identical to routine flakiness and gets the same dismissive treatment — the suite keeps running but stops providing actual safety. This is a real risk, not a harmless outcome or merely wasted compute, and it has nothing to do with the test framework itself breaking.
